addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][M] (done)
- [[N]] [<title>][M] (current)
- [[N]] [<title>][M]
- [[N]] <cycle title> closing

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<one `#####` subsection per rung, headed by its exact title, opened at laddering with the
rung's intent and completed at landing with the conceptual delta; the closing rung's only at
close-out, gotchas in problem/solution form>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Problem

Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
`.agent-session`.

# custom-family.md - vc-x1's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family

Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
member repo. A project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies
to one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `vc-x1` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name `vc-x1`).
Versioning specifics are in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)), not a compatibility
contract. The crate has no library target, but the built CLI has external consumers (the family's
repos run it), so a change that breaks an existing invocation or the `.vc-config.toml` schema is
called out in the commit and surfaced by the tool's own errors rather than promised by the
version. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

**Single-name convention** (adopted at the 0.78.3 cycle): the package name is the binary's
name, `vc-x1` on `main`, with per-line dev names on long-lived branches, guarded by `build.rs`
on every cargo verb. This is the project's answer to versioning.md's
[Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name): the repo is striving to
release, so `main` builds install as plain `vc-x1`.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5 (skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out)
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

## Membership

- **member name**: `vc-x1`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know, so a config carrying them would fail its own validator. The
`[private]` table proposal tracks the fix.

## Messaging

Members leave word for each other in per-member mailboxes at the template repository. The protocol
is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md` and it governs. These are the parts that decide how a session
behaves.

- **At acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md`.** An absent file means no mail.
- **Handle, then delete** the entry, and delete the file once it empties. Mailboxes hold open
  items only.
- **So a message can never be a record.** Anything in one worth keeping is copied into
  `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` *before* the entry is deleted.
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state.** Durable coordination state lives in topical files. A
  message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo.** A repo with a live session is written
  only by its own agent.

## Dogfood log

This project's log lives in [notes/dogfood.md](notes/dogfood.md): dated entries on where the
pinned instructions chafed, failed, or got amended, the evidence base for the family's
convergence decisions ([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). It stays
a separate file because it predates this one and is long. In-flight entries only: a resolved
entry retires at the beat where it resolves, per
[Retiring Done entries](agent-data/notes.md#retiring-done-entries).

61	#### Solution
62	
63	Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
64	config surface from it:
65	
66	- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
67	  reference url
68	- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
69	  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
70	  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
71	    code cannot disagree with the file
72	- each key's rendered block carries a `doc references:` list: the derived web url (a
73	  localfile entry joins at backlog #52, once init seeds the file it would point at)
74	- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
75	- retire the state-dir leftovers
76	- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
77	  active keys and `[repos]`
78	  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
79	    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
80	- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
81	  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
82	  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
83	- repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`
84	  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
85	    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record
86	
87	#### Acceptance check
88	
89	1. build.rs generates the schema table and default constants from `vc-config.toml`
90	   (rerun-if-changed wired), the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP` constants are gone
91	   from `src/`, and generated configs carry each key's `doc references:` list (the derived web
92	   url per key).
93	2. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
94	   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
95	3. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
96	   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
97	4. `config --refresh --check` exits clean on both sides, proving the committed config files
98	   match what the prototype renders.
99	5. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
100	   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
101	6. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
102	   dir under its new name.
103	7. `validate-anchors` runs clean over `TODO.md`, `notes/`, `README.md`, and `vc-config.md`
104	   (same-file heading anchors and `[N]` refs), and a test shows it catching a broken anchor.
105

111	- [[N]] [docs: ladder ToC + per-rung sections][36] (done)
112	- [[N]] [docs: amend cycle conventions][37] (done)
113	- [[N]] [feat: per-key doc references][38]
114	- [[N]] [chore: regenerate stale config files][39]
115	- [[N]] [feat: add config --refresh][40]
116	- [[N]] [feat: add validate-anchors][41]

#### Solution

Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
config surface from it:

- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
  reference url
- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
    code cannot disagree with the file
- each key's rendered block carries a `doc references:` list: the derived web url (a
  localfile entry joins at backlog #52, once init seeds the file it would point at)
- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
- retire the state-dir leftovers
- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
  active keys and `[repos]`
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
- repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`
  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record

#### Acceptance check

1. build.rs generates the schema table and default constants from `vc-config.toml`
   (rerun-if-changed wired), the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP` constants are gone
   from `src/`, and generated configs carry each key's `doc references:` list (the derived web
   url per key).
2. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
3. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
4. `config --refresh --check` exits clean on both sides, proving the committed config files
   match what the prototype renders.
5. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
6. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
   dir under its new name.
7. `validate-anchors` runs clean over `TODO.md`, `notes/`, `README.md`, and `vc-config.md`
   (same-file heading anchors and `[N]` refs), and a test shows it catching a broken anchor.

content.text:
I've re-read the in-progress block and backlog #52. Here's my assessment of the `.vc-config.md` idea.

**What it actually solves.** The gap that forced the `localfile://` cut was: inside a `.toml` file, everything is `#` comments, and no editor linkifies a relative path in a comment. The web url survives because terminals and editors linkify bare `https://` anywhere. Your move dissolves the problem instead of patching it: if the instance config *is* markdown, then `[1]: ./vc-config.md#bot-sessioncol-width` is a real markdown reference link, and every renderer we measured for backlog #53 (GitHub, VS Code preview, Zed with its quirks) already knows how to follow it. No taught handler, no custom scheme. That is a genuine improvement over `localfile://`, which needed per-editor teaching and was "harder in zed" even then.

**What it doesn't change.** The link still points at a file that has to exist in the member, so the dependency on #52's seeding (init distributes `vc-config.md`, stamps `reference-base`) is unchanged. The md-config removes the handler problem, not the seeding problem.

**The real costs, as I see them:**

1. **Two config dialects.** Loader, `config --validate`, the upcoming `config --refresh` / `--check`, drift tests, and `init` all grow a second surface. Which file wins when both exist has to be defined (I'd say: both present is an error, not a precedence rule).
2. **Parsing and error mapping.** Extract-and-concatenate the ```toml fences, then parse; TOML error line numbers no longer match file lines, so the loader needs a fence-offset map to keep `--validate` messages pointing at the right line.
3. **Lost TOML tooling.** taplo/LSP won't run inside fences. Syntax highlighting survives (fences are language-tagged), and our schema comments were always doing the LSP's job anyway, so this cost is small here.
4. **Refresh gets easier, not harder.** Today's `--refresh` design rewrites commented schema blocks while preserving active keys and `[repos]`. In the md form the boundary is structural: prose sections are generated, fence interiors are the user's. That's a cleaner preserve/replace line than "comment block vs uncommented key".

There's solid precedent for the shape: Rust's RFC 3503 embeds a Cargo manifest as a fenced `toml` block in a script file, and Python's PEP 723 does the same; fenced-toml-in-a-host-document is an established pattern, not an invention.

**Where it belongs.** This is scope beyond the current rung: rung 38 (`feat: per-key doc references`) is deliberately web-url-only, and the cycle conventions say a mid-feature design itch becomes a backlog entry, not an inserted rung. My recommendation: record it as a new backlog entry ("support .vc-config.md as a markdown instance config"), cross-linked to #52 and #53, noting it likely *supersedes* the `localfile://` plan in #52 (the append-only list slot #52 reserved would instead be a `[N]`-style reference in the md form). The natural decision point is the "chore: regenerate stale config files" rung, where #52's ownership model is already slated to be settled.

One design question to hold onto for that entry: whether `.vc-config.md` becomes the *only* format eventually (migration, one dialect, no precedence question) or a permanent alternative (adopters who want plain toml keep it). My lean is migrate-to-one: the family's whole instinct is single-dialect (see the revset decision in the mailbox), and two formats forever means every config feature is built twice.

The plain version: your markdown-config idea fixes the clickable-local-link problem better than the `localfile://` scheme we cut, because markdown links just work everywhere markdown renders. It costs a second file format to support, which argues for eventually making it the only format. I'd write it up as a backlog entry linked to #52/#53 and decide its fate at the regenerate rung. Want me to draft that entry?

message.content: Actually, you right we only need one format, but internally to process the .md file I link we'd call a filter function which returns a string in .toml format.

content.text:
That's the right internal shape, and it keeps the change small: one filter at the loader boundary, `md_to_toml(&str) -> String` (or `-> Result` with positions), and everything downstream — serde parse, validation, defaults — stays exactly as it is today, toml-native and format-blind. The rest of the codebase never learns markdown exists.

Two details worth pinning in the design so the filter stays honest:

1. **Preserve line numbers instead of mapping them.** If the filter emits the file with non-fence lines *blanked* rather than removed — every prose line becomes an empty line, fence interiors pass through verbatim — the returned string has the same line count as the source, and TOML parse errors point at the correct line of `.vc-config.md` with zero mapping machinery. Concatenate-and-offset-map works too, but blank-line preservation gets the same result for free.

2. **Fence recognition should be dumb on purpose.** A line scanner that tracks ``` fence state and takes only fences tagged `toml` is about twenty lines and has no failure modes a markdown library would save us from. It should ignore untagged and non-toml fences (so the doc prose can show shell examples), and treat an unclosed fence as an error rather than silently swallowing the rest of the file.

A pleasant consequence for `--refresh`: since fence interiors are the only lines the filter reads, "user-owned" has a mechanical definition — refresh regenerates all prose, preserves fence interiors byte-for-byte, and there's no comment-block heuristic left to get wrong.

One choice the filter forces into the open: whether multiple `toml` fences concatenate into one document (each key's section carries its own small fence, like your sketch) or one fence holds the whole config. Your sketch's per-section fences read better and concatenation is trivial with blanking, so I'd spec multiple-fences-concatenate from the start.

The plain version: yes — a small function turns the markdown into a toml string at the front door and nothing else in the program changes. If it blanks the prose lines instead of deleting them, error messages line up with the real file for free.

I'll draft the backlog entry with this internal design folded in whenever you say.

Thinking it through, I land where you do, and the deciding fact is where the cycle happens to be standing.

**The pivot point is unusually clean.** Everything landed so far survives untouched: the prototype `vc-config.toml` stays the build source, the build.rs codegen stays, the ladder/records conventions work stays. The format switch only changes the *rendered instance*, and every rung that renders it is still ahead of us. Which means the alternative — finish the cycle as laddered, then switch formats next cycle — has us building the comment-block renderer (rung 38), regenerating toml-form files (39), and writing the comment-block-preserving `--refresh` heuristic (40), all of which the md format deletes. Rung 40 is the sharpest case: its entire difficulty is telling generated comment blocks from user-owned keys, and in md form that problem doesn't exist — fence interiors are the user's, prose is the generator's, byte-for-byte. Deferring means building the hard version of a thing whose easy version we've already designed.

**The title covers it honestly.** "Freshen vc-config" is exactly what this is; nobody reading the history would feel the cycle outgrew its name. This isn't an inserted convention itch, it's the cycle's own subject matter getting a better answer mid-flight. The protocol-clean move is a Preparation-grade revision: rewrite the Solution, Acceptance check, and rungs 38-42 in the In Progress block, record the pivot and its reasoning in Deliberation, and go. The six items are explicitly provisional and "revised as steps land" — this is what that clause is for.

Three things I'd want settled at that revision, because they're real decisions rather than mechanics:

1. **The name collision.** The instance config becomes `.vc-config.md` while the seeded family doc (#52) is `vc-config.md` — two markdown files differing by a dot, one per-member values, one pinned doc. That's a foot-gun for exactly the neophyte we're serving. Worth deciding eyes-open: keep both names, rename the doc, or ask whether the md-form config absorbs enough per-key doc that #52's seeded copy shrinks to the fuller prose and examples only.
2. **Version scope.** The deliberation pinned this cycle at patch 0.78.8, and 0.79.0 is spoken for by the trapezoid branch. Replacing the config file format is the schema-breaking species of change the family watches for; it reads bigger than a patch. Needs your call on how the numbers shake out.
3. **Cutover for the other members.** One format as the end state, but iiac-perf and the template carry `.vc-config.toml` today and run this binary. Smallest honest transition: the loader reads `.md`, errors helpfully on finding only `.toml` ("run config --migrate" or a mailbox note), and we coordinate the family's migration through the mailboxes. The family is three repos; a hard cutover with mail is cheaper than a compatibility window.

One mild caution to keep us honest: "superior in every way" is almost true, but the toml form did have one virtue the md form gives up — the instance file was directly editable with TOML tooling (taplo, LSP) and trivially parseable by any third-party tool that wants to read a member's config. Fenced toml is still readable by anything that strips fences, so the cost is small, but it's not zero and the records should say we saw it.

The plain version: yes, do it now — this is the last moment where the switch costs nothing already built and saves the hardest work still ahead. Before starting, revise the cycle's records to say so, and settle three things: the near-identical filenames of config and doc, what version number this now deserves, and how the other family repos migrate.

content.text:
Read it. The single-table shape at the top is uncontroversial; the interesting part is the per-key shape, and there's one real problem in it.

**`[[bot-session]]` doesn't mean what the file needs it to mean.** In TOML, `[[x]]` is array-of-tables: three fences of `[[bot-session]]` concatenate into an *array* of three one-key tables, not one table with three keys. It's legal TOML, which is the trap — it parses fine and then hands downstream a `Vec<Table>` where serde expects a table, so the "filter returns a toml string, nothing downstream changes" property dies; something has to fold the array back into one table and decide what duplicate keys mean. And to anyone who knows TOML, the file reads as declaring an array, which we don't mean. (I'd guess this was reaching for a way around the real constraint: plain `[bot-session]` repeated across fences is a "table redefined" error, so *some* trick is needed for per-key fences.)

**The trick that works is dotted keys.** TOML allows root-level dotted assignments to the same super-table any number of times:

```toml
bot-session.col-width = 68
```

Each fence like that is valid standalone, the concatenation is valid, and the parse result is *identical* to the `[bot-session]` table form — downstream code can't tell the difference, no merge step, no new semantics. It's also arguably better for this file's purpose: the fence names the full key (`bot-session.col-width`), exactly matching the doc anchor it sits next to, with no header context the reader has to scroll up for.

The one wrinkle dotted keys bring: TOML forbids *mixing* — once `bot-session.x` is set at root, a later `[bot-session]` header is a redefinition error. So the format should commit to one idiom for the generated file, and I'd make it dotted keys throughout, `[repos]` included (`repos.work = "."` is fine). A user who prefers to consolidate into one `[bot-session]` header fence can, as long as that's the only place the table appears — the concatenation-must-parse rule catches violations loudly, which is the failure mode we want.

Smaller notes on the file:

- The anchors (`#bot-sessioncol-width`, dots stripped) match GitHub's slugging, and the `validate-anchors` rung will be able to check them mechanically — the reference-link form is pulling its weight here.
- The generated per-key block should carry the doc one-liner as prose above the fence (what today's `#` comment block says), not just the bare key name and `[[N]]` — that's the neophyte's first read; the link is the second.
- `test-vc-config.md` at the repo root will want a home before the rung lands — my suggestion: it becomes the filter's test fixture more or less as-is, since it usefully holds both shapes (and, amended, the mixing error case).

On your three decisions: agreed on all, and one follow-on each. The `vc-config-design.md` rename frees both names, but I'd still pick exactly one for the instance — my lean is the visible `vc-config.md`, since a discoverable, GitHub-rendered file at the root is the whole neophyte story, and error if both a config `.md` and `.toml` are present rather than defining precedence. On versioning, aligned — nothing is spoken for until it lands on `main`; the Deliberation line saying 0.79.0 is spoken for should be corrected when we revise the records. And keeping `.toml` valid is nearly free given the pipeline (the filter just doesn't run), so no argument there.

The plain version: the per-key idea is right but the double-bracket syntax accidentally declares a list; writing each key as `bot-session.col-width = 68` instead gets the same per-key layout with zero downstream cost. Commit the format to that dotted style, keep your test file as the parser's test fixture, and pick one filename for the config — I'd go with the visible `vc-config.md`.

Before any header, the same line is at the root and means what we want. Since no syntax ever closes a header's scope, a file that opens any `[header]` can never define root-level keys again — which is exactly why the generated format should be dotted-keys-only, no headers ever.

It makes a difference, but not the one you'd want. Look at the parse: your three real keys did land in `bot-session` (the header fence put them there directly), but the dotted fences all got swallowed into `end-bot-session.bot-session.*` — the marker table became their parent. And the config now also carries a spurious `end-bot-session` table. No parse error, so we're back in the silent-garbage failure mode, just with a different shape of garbage.

The underlying fact is that TOML simply has no "return to root" syntax. `[end-bot-session]` is not a terminator, it's a declaration of a table literally named `end-bot-session`, and everything after it belongs to that table just as everything after `[bot-session]` belonged to that one. People have asked the TOML spec for exactly this — some way to pop back to the root — and it's never been added. The root table is only writable before the first header in the document, full stop.

So the three experiments now cover the whole space:

- header then dotted: parses, silently nests under `bot-session.bot-session`
- dotted then header: loud "declared twice" error
- header, marker, then dotted: parses, silently nests under `end-bot-session.bot-session`

All three say the same thing: headers and per-key dotted fences cannot coexist in a concatenated document by any ordering or trick. The format's rule stays what we said, and now it's evidence-backed rather than asserted: fences contain root-level dotted keys only, headers are forbidden, and the filter can enforce that cheaply — reject any fence line starting with `[` before the TOML parser even runs, so the user gets "no table headers in vc-config.md, use bot-session.key = ..." instead of whichever of the three confusing outcomes above their ordering happened to produce.

The plain version: there is no way to end a table in TOML — a `[whatever]` line just starts another table and captures everything after it, so your end-marker quietly stole the dotted keys into itself. Headers can't be made to work in this format by any arrangement; the fix is the rule we already had — dotted keys only — plus having the filter reject `[` lines outright with a helpful message.

content.text:
Here's the full picture, and it lands where the earlier discussion guessed — workable, but strictly worse than dotted keys.

**Pure `[[bot-session]]` fences** (one per key) parse cleanly in any order into an *array* of one-key tables: `[{'items': ...}, {'result-lines': ...}, {'col-width': ...}]`. The failure is loud at least — serde would reject "array where table expected" — but to make it work we'd have to write a merge step that folds the array into one table. That merge is where the trouble concentrates, because of the fourth case above: **the same key set in two fences parses without complaint** as two array entries. TOML's own duplicate-key protection doesn't apply across array elements, so "you set `col-width` twice" becomes *our* code, our error message, our choice of error-vs-last-wins. Compare dotted keys, where the third case shows TOML itself refusing a duplicate (`Cannot overwrite a value`) with a line number, for free.

**Mixing** is as hazardous as ever: dotted-then-array errors loudly, array-then-dotted silently nests the dotted key inside the last array element (second case — same swallowing behavior as the `[end-bot-session]` experiment, because `[[x]]` opens a scope that runs to the next header too).

So the scorecard, array-of-tables versus dotted keys:

- one extra `[[bot-session]]` boilerplate line per fence, versus none
- semantics that read as "a list of bot-sessions" to any TOML-literate reader or third-party tool, versus exactly what we mean
- a hand-written merge layer with hand-written duplicate detection, versus TOML doing both natively
- downstream serde config type changes (or a pre-merge pass), versus byte-identical to today's parse

Dotted keys win every row; the array form's only virtue is that its pure form can't silently mis-nest among *themselves*, and dotted fences share that virtue anyway. I'd stay with `bot-session.col-width = 68` as the format's one idiom, and keep the filter's "reject any fence line starting with `[`" rule — it conveniently bans both headers and array-of-tables with one check.

One housekeeping note: your latest edit isn't on disk yet — the file still reads as the `[end-bot-session]` revision, so save when you get a chance and I'll check what you actually wrote against all this.

The plain version: double-bracket fences do parse in any order, but they build a list that we'd have to flatten ourselves, and TOML stops checking for duplicate keys the moment you use them. The dotted form keeps every safety TOML offers and needs no extra code, so it stays the recommendation.

I was guarding against headers because of the mixing hazards we explored, but test2 doesn't mix — it uses the header *as* the technique, deliberately: one tiny `[bot-session]` fence opens the scope, and every key fence after it is a clean bare `col-width = 68` with its doc line and `[[N]]` link right above it. That's per-key adjacency (the whole point of the md format) with none of the dotted form's `bot-session.` prefix noise repeated on every line. It's your `[end-bot-session]` insight — headers capture everything after them — aimed correctly, same as the `bot-session-list` experiment.

Test2's one real cost is what dotted keys had for free: **the key fences are order-dependent**. A bare `items = ...` fence means nothing on its own; it means "items in whichever table's header is most recently above me." Today that's harmless — one settings table. The day the file carries `[repos]` too, a key fence appended at the bottom silently belongs to `[repos]`, and the failure surfaces as an unknown-key validation error naming the wrong table ("unknown key `col-width` in `[repos]`"), which is loud but momentarily confusing. Two cheap mitigations: the generator always emits each table as one contiguous region, header first; and the unknown-key error can append a hint ("keys belong to the nearest `[table]` fence above them") since the filter knows the file was markdown.

Test3 needs no "support" decision at all — it's what a user who wants compactness collapses to, it parses identically under the same filter, and the format spec can bless both with one sentence: *the `toml` fences, concatenated in document order, must form a valid config.* That single rule is the format. Dotted keys also remain legal under it automatically, and my earlier "reject `[` lines in fences" rule is withdrawn — it belonged to the dotted-only design and would ban test2's technique.

For `--refresh`, test2 also has the cleanest story: fence interiors are preserved verbatim (the header fence included), and only the prose between them regenerates — the reference definitions at the bottom being generated prose too.

The plain version: both of your layouts already work under the one dumb rule "glue the toml fences together and parse" — I ran the real filter on the real files to prove it. Your test2 lean is right: the lone header fence up top plus bare per-key fences reads best and matches how the docs attach to keys. Its only trap — a key fence added below the wrong header joins the wrong table — stays theoretical until a second table exists, and validation catches it loudly even then.

# vc-config.toml: the schema PROTOTYPE, not a config file.
#
# This file is the single source of truth for vc-x1's settable
# config keys. build.rs parses it and generates the schema table
# and default constants the binary is compiled from, so the code
# cannot disagree with this file. Your workspace config is
# `.vc-config.toml` (note the leading dot); editing THIS file
# changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build,
# and is reviewed like any source change.
#
# Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path
# (dynamic segments quoted: [repo.category."<cat>"]). Entries:
#
#   homes      which config file(s) accept the key: "user"
#              (~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml), "workspace-code",
#              "workspace-bot" (the two .vc-config.toml sides)
#   kind       value shape: "str", "usize", or "item-list"
#   doc        one-line description (rendered, keep it tight)
#   used-by    the command/flag or structural context consuming it
#   default    the built-in value; omit when there is none
#   example    representative value for keys with no default
#   required   active (not commented) in generated configs; the
#              value is role-specific, filled by init
#   reference  optional override url for the key's docs; when
#              absent (the norm) build.rs derives
#              <reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of
#              the path>, the key's section in vc-config.md on the
#              repo's default branch

# Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream.

# settable key.
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"

[default.account]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use when --account is absent"
used-by = "--account (init and account-aware commands)"
example = "work"

[default.debug]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default --debug value when used without an argument (reserved; not yet consumed)"
used-by = "--debug (reserved; not yet consumed)"
example = "true"

[repo.default]

kind = "str"
doc = "Default repo category when --repo is bare: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"

example = "acmehousing"

[repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]

content.text:
Now I can see the whole board, and the two moves are better than you're giving them credit for — with one amendment on the design doc's fate.

**The prototype in md format: yes, and it's the keystone move.** Look at what falls out. The derived web url that build.rs stamps into every generated doc-reference is `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor>` — a name that just came free. If the prototype takes it, in md form with one `## <key-path>` heading per key, then the prototype *is* the anchor target: every reference link in every member's config lands on the key's section in the schema source itself, where the fence shows `doc`, `default`, `used-by`, `homes` — exactly what a browsing neophyte wants, rendered by GitHub as tidy toml blocks. The derive doesn't even change; the name it always pointed at becomes real. The prototype's compact one-table-per-key fences are the self-contained style, so no region hazards, and the filter is the same fifteen lines shared with the instance loader (build.rs pulling it in via a small shared module is routine plumbing).

**Which leads to the amendment: `vc-config-design.md` shouldn't move to notes/ — it should mostly cease to exist.** I checked its structure: it's not a design doc, it's a per-key reference — twelve `## <key>` sections, the very anchor targets the test files link to. Under the prototype-as-md plan, every one of those sections merges into the prototype's per-key sections (its prose becomes the section body above each schema fence), and the file has nothing left. Merging beats moving for three reasons: one per-key doc surface instead of two that drift apart; backlog #52 ("init distributes vc-config.md") now distributes a file that is simultaneously the doc *and* the schema the binary was built from, which is the strongest possible byte-identity story; and notes/ is the wrong home anyway for anything user-facing — it's records, not reference, and a doc that init distributes and web urls target can't live there. If any genuinely design-flavored narrative accumulates (this format's spec, the ownership model), *that* residue is what earns a notes/ file — or better, a short "format" section at the top of vc-config.md itself, since the file's own header comment already plays that role today.

So the end state I'd argue for: **`vc-config.md`** = prototype + reference doc, one file, filter-parsed by build.rs, distributed by init, anchor target of every link. **`.vc-config.md`** = the dotted instance in each repo side, generated from it. **`.vc-config.toml`** = still accepted by the loader for the transition. **`vc-config-design.md`** = merged away. The naming symmetry with the toml era is exact — visible file is schema-and-doc, dotted file is your values — which is one less thing to reteach.

Two loose ends for the records revision when we pivot: `reference-base` currently lives in the prototype's `[vc-config]` table, and #52 wants init to stamp it per member — that table rides along into the md prototype unchanged, just worth naming. And the three `test*-vc-config.md` files at the root should be swept into fixtures when the filter lands, so the root doesn't accumulate experiments.

The plain version: turning the prototype into `vc-config.md` is even better than it looks, because the generated links already point at that filename — the schema file becomes the documentation the links open. And rather than moving the old doc into notes/, fold its per-key sections into the new file and delete it: two documents describing the same keys will always drift, and one document that is both the source of truth and the thing you browse can't.

content.text:
Now table1. The short answer on how it would be parsed: **under the format we've built, it wouldn't be** — the filter extracts `toml` fences, table1 has none, so it yields an empty document and a "no config found" error. The real question is what it would take to *make* it parse, and that's where the assessment gets interesting, because the file quietly demonstrates every convention we'd have to invent:

1. **The table's name lives in prose.** Nothing machine-readable binds `| work= | ... |` to `[repos]` — the binding is the English sentence above it, with the name in a backtick span. We'd need a rule like "nearest preceding inline code containing `[...]`" (fragile) or a required heading form (rigid). The fence format never has this problem: the header is *inside* the parsed text.
2. **Cell syntax is ours to define.** `` `work=` `` carries a cosmetic `=` to strip; values like `"."` are TOML fragments needing a per-cell mini-parse; and a string value containing `|` breaks the table itself unless the user knows to write `\|`. Item-list values with long strings will also fight the column grid hard.
3. **We'd be parsing markdown for real.** Pipe tables have dialect quirks (alignment rows, optional outer pipes), so the fifteen-line line-scanner becomes a dependency on a markdown parser plus a table-walker — call it ten times the code.
4. **TOML's native protections vanish.** Duplicate keys, type mismatches, bad escapes — all currently caught by the TOML parser with line numbers — become our hand-written checks and messages, the same cost that sank array-of-tables, but larger.

The pattern underneath: the fence format has a one-sentence spec because *TOML supplies all the semantics* — markdown is just the carrier. Table1 inverts that: markdown becomes the syntax, and every semantic rule (name binding, cell grammar, escaping) is a new invention we'd document, teach, and maintain forever. It's a bespoke config DSL wearing markdown's clothes.

And yet — the file reads wonderfully, and that's worth keeping. The place tables belong is the *generated, read-only* side: `vc-config.md` (the prototype-as-doc) can open each table's section with a generated summary grid exactly like table1's — key, default, docs link — as presentation over the fences that remain the parse source. Same for any rendered per-key overview. Tables for reading, fences for meaning: each format doing the one job it's good at, and the parser never learns markdown tables exist.

Two small notes from the files themselves: you've started prototyping the neutral naming in these drafts (`repos.agent`, `[agent-session]`) — reference `[5]` still points at `#reposbot`, one to sweep when these become real. And `test-vc-config.md` and `test3-vc-config.md` are deleted as decided; `test2-vc-config.md` (all-compact now) and `table1-vc-config.md` remain at the root.

The plain version: the table file can't be parsed by the format we designed, and making it parseable would mean inventing a small new language — name-binding rules, cell grammar, escaping — to replace work TOML already does for free. But the layout is genuinely the nicest to read, so use it where nothing parses it: as generated summary tables in the documentation, while the config people edit stays in the fence format test2 models.

message.content: Your thoughts on "agent" vs "bot"

content.text:
My take: "agent" is the right word, and the family is already halfway there without having noticed.

**The vocabulary is currently split down the middle.** On one side: `AGENTS.md`, agent-files, `agent-data/` — the instruction surface has been agent-vocabulary from the start, and `AGENTS.md` isn't even our choice, it's the cross-tool convention the whole ecosystem settled on. On the other side: bot repo, `repos.bot`, `[bot-session]`, `--scope=bot`, "the rules bind the bot." Two words for one actor, and the split line is arbitrary — it just marks which era each name was coined in. Consolidating on "agent" makes the family speak one language; consolidating on "bot" would mean renaming `AGENTS.md` against an external convention, which is not on the table. So the direction is really already decided; the question is only how far and when.

**The rename rung already forced the issue.** `.agent-session` is the agreed new directory name. The moment that lands, `repos.bot = ".agent-session"` is a config whose key contradicts its value, and prose saying "bot repo" labels a directory named agent-session. Your drafts (`repos.agent`, `[agent-session]`) are just making the config keys tell the same story as the path they point at.

**On the merits of the words themselves**: "bot" has brevity going for it and not much else — its connotation is spam and dumb automation, which undersells what the sessions actually are, and it reads as our private dialect where "agent" reads as the industry's. The one real cost of "agent" is a new ambiguity: "agent-files" (the instructions, in the work repo) versus "agent repo" (the session data) now share a prefix, where "bot repo" was lexically distinct. I think it's minor — both are defined terms in AGENTS.md's Terminology, and the hyphenation rule already disambiguates — but it's the one thing "bot" did better, and the records should say we saw it.

**On sequencing, which is the real decision**: split it at the config/prose boundary.

- *This cycle*: the machine surface — `repos.agent`, `[agent-session]`, the directory itself, and whatever the `bot-session` subcommand becomes (an `agent-session` name with the old one kept as a hidden alias for a transition window, since `--scope=bot` and the subcommand are external invocation surfaces the family's own repos use). The justification is that this cycle *is already* the config migration: format change, file rename, key regeneration. Riding the vocabulary flip on the same wave means the family migrates once, not twice. Doing keys now and names next cycle would ship `repos.bot` into the brand-new format only to break it again.
- *Its own small cycle later*: the prose sweep — AGENTS.md's Terminology section, jj.md, the checklists, all pinned family files where the change is a convergence proposal per rule 12. "Bot" gets a retirement line in Terminology exactly like "instruction files" got one. Convention work runs as its own cycle, and this sweep is pure convention.

The interim dissonance (config says agent, some prose still says bot) is real but already unavoidable — the directory rename creates it regardless — and a Terminology line noting "bot: being retired in favor of agent, sweep pending" makes it a documented transition instead of drift.

The plain version: go with "agent" — half the project already says it, the ecosystem's `AGENTS.md` convention locks it in, and the new directory name demands it. Flip the config keys and CLI names in this cycle while the config is already migrating, and sweep the prose in a small dedicated cycle afterward, with old names kept as aliases long enough for the family to move.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## File reads: read the slice you need
13	
14	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
15	further on demand.
16	
17	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
18	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
19	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
20	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
21	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
22	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
23	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
24	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
25	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
26	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
27	  need.
28	
29	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
30	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
31	to historical files.
32	
33	## Notes references
34	
35	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
36	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
37	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
38	single-bracketed.
39	
40	## Reference numbering
41	
42	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
43	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
44	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
45	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
46	
47	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
48	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
49	file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
50	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
51	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
52	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
53	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
54	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
55	
56	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
57	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
58	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
59	as-built ladder, or a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own
60	subsection. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
61	exact shape.
62	
63	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
64	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
65	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
66	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
67	definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
68	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
69	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
70	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
71	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
72	slots out of document order).
73	
74	## Markdown anchor links
75	
76	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
77	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
78	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
79	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
80	official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
81	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
82	
83	## Todo format
84	
85	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
86	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
87	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
88	description with reference links to more detail.
89	
90	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
91	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
92	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
93	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
94	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
95	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
96	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
97	
98	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
99	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
100	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
101	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
102	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
103	
104	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
105	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
106	
107	Example shape:
108	
109	```
110	# Todo
111	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
112	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
113	
114	# Done
115	- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]
116	
117	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
118	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
119	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
120	```
121	
122	## Done entry form
123	
124	A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
125	title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:
126	
127	```
128	- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
129	  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
130	  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
131	```
132	
133	- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
134	  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
135	  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
136	  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
137	  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
138	- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
139	  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
140	  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
141	  line, trades one of those for the other. See
142	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
143	  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
144	- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
145	  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
146	- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
147	  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
148	- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
149	  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.
150	
151	## Retiring Done entries
152	
153	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
154	log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:
155	
156	- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
157	  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
158	  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
159	- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
160	  version-of-record.
161	- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
162	  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
163	  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
164	  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
165	  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).
166	
167	Migration mechanics:
168	
169	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
170	  number).
171	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
172	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
173	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
174	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
175	
176	## Chores conventions
177	
178	### Headings and entries that record a commit
179	
180	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
181	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
182	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
183	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
184	version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
185	are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
186	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
187	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
188	`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
189	(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
190	[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
191	[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).
192	
193	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
194	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
195	whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
196	commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
197	match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
198	record up with its commit.
199	
200	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
201	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
202	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
203	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
204	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
205	
206	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
207	free-form text. The convention applies going forward.
208	
209	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
210	
211	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
212	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
213	design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
214	rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
215	**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
216	changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
217	body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
218	source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others; none
219	restates another.
220	
221	The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
222	`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
223	narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
224	than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
225	[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
226	two don't drift.
227	
228	**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
229	chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
230	drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.
231	
232	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
233	Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
234	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
235	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
236	direction).
237	
238	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
239	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
240	and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
241	
242	### Chores commit references
243	
244	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
245	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
246	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
247	one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:
248	
249	```
250	## refactor: extract config loader
251	
252	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
253	- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader
254	
255	<intro paragraph...>
256	```
257	
258	- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
259	  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
260	  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment
261	  (`[M]: #<slug>`): it rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the
262	  subsections move into the same file, renumbered like any other slot (the closing rung is
263	  unlinked unless close-out gotchas gave it a subsection). No step number and no
264	  `(current)` / `(done)` marker,
265	  since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
266	  Landing order is the list order. See
267	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
268	- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
269	  (see
270	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
271	  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
272	  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
273	  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
274	  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
275	  falsify.
276	- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
277	  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
278	  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
279	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
280	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
281	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
282	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
283	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
284	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
285	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
286	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
287	
288	```
289	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
290	```
291	
292	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
293	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
294	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
295	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
296	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
297	
298	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
299	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
300	is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
301	opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
302	the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
303	lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
304	cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
305	
306	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
307	going forward.
308	
309	### Chores file Table of Contents
310	
311	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
312	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
313	section, in file order.
314	
315	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
316	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
317	- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
318	  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
319	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
320	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
321
