`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
as-built ladder, or a **same-file fragment**, `[N]: #<slug>`, a ladder rung's link to its own
subsection. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
exact shape.

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
slots out of document order).

## Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

## Todo format

`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
description with reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Done entry form

A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:

```
- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
```

- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
  line, trades one of those for the other. See
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.
- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title
(the chores header's bare form, not the suffixed closing commit's: see
[Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), and its shape is in
[Done entry form](#done-entry-form).

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text. The convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others; none
restates another.

The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
two don't drift.

**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 [refactor: split loader from parser][4]
- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment
  (`[M]: #<slug>`): it rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the
  subsections move into the same file, renumbered like any other slot (the closing rung is
  unlinked unless close-out gotchas gave it a subsection). No step number and no
  `(current)` / `(done)` marker,
  since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
  Landing order is the list order. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
  falsify.
- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

202	block, rung-titled headings intact. Depth note: under a program heading the subsections sit at
203	markdown's heading floor while the block is in `TODO.md`; the close-out move shifts the block
204	shallower, so the chores copy has room.
205	
206	Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
207	section is created at close-out by moving this block. See
208	[Chores sections](#chores-sections).
209	
210	**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
211	cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
212	banner claim is false: a seven-cycle program opened against
213	"end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed the goal
214	met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two inside the
215	facade the program built. Being provisional, the check can
216	also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
217	same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is one of
218	the things the deliberation exists to justify.
219	
220	## Work-N
221	
222	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
223	implement the change. As many as needed:
224	
225	- Each commit runs through the
226	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
227	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
228	  visibility).
229	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
230	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
231	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
232	  scope grows enough (see
233	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
234	
235	## Close-out
236	
237	The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the
238	commit body describes that bookkeeping, not what happens
239	post-squash:
240	
241	- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
242	  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
243	  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
244	  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
245	  quietly restate the banner.
246	- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
247	  the title if the cycle's scope shifted (and every anchor
248	  back-reference), replace the provisional solution
249	  statement with what was actually done, drop the ladder's
250	  `(current)` / `(done)` markers since as-built implies
251	  done, and add any design subsections the deliberation
252	  grew. The `Ladder details` subsections ride the move
253	  unchanged.
254	- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
255	  applying the four transforms in
256	  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
257	  section. Nothing was opened earlier.
258	- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
259	  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
260	  sub-bullets (see
261	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
262	- **Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block** with
263	  `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
264	  program (the program heading above the cycle title) this
265	  retires the cycle's block only. The program heading and
266	  its ladder stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the
267	  marker sits inside the program block until the next stage
268	  is picked up.
269	- **Land the cycle's bookmark** on the user's go (commands
270	  in [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
271	  Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. Landing
272	  triggers the backfill that waits on permanence.
273	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
274	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
275	
276	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
277	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time. See
278	[Pushing](#pushing).
279	
280	## Step naming
281	
282	A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs
283	in order, so position is already recorded by the list, and a
284	step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the
285	ladder rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
286	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
287	A title has to be unambiguous within its cycle and within
288	its chores file, where it is also an anchor. It may repeat
289	across the repo's history.
290	
291	The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its
292	suffix still encodes the phase, but that encoding belongs to
293	the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one
294	number left in the system, it names nothing, and nothing
295	dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
296	optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
297	format, and the per-step bump) lives in
298	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the
299	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
300	
301	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
302	
303	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent
304	branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes the work durable and
305	visible; it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent
306	branch is publication, and that is the line the rules divide
307	at:
308	
309	- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent
310	  when practical. Inserting or reordering a step changes the
311	  ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older
312	  version of it are brought along, so the branch reads as
313	  one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it was
314	  assembled.
315	- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not
316	  touched. A recorded SHA is only ever written for a commit
317	  on a permanent branch (see
318	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which is what
319	  makes rewriting a draft safe.
320	
321	Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:
322	
323	- **Amend content; never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md`
324	  inside a rung and amending it is not a `jj describe`, so
325	  the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers
326	  survive, since they carry change ids rather than commit
327	  ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
328	- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same
329	  approval any push needs.
330	- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always":
331	  the bookmark has already landed; another branch is stacked
332	  on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or
333	  the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
334	  Name the reason and move on.
335	
336	A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never
337	meets this, because nothing on it is pushed and the
338	close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the
339	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time.
340	
341	## Per-commit flow
342	
343	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
344	through:
345	
346	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
347	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
348	   root).
349	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
350	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
351	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
352	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit. Write
353	   the rung's `Ladder details` subsection now, when it has
354	   conceptual content (see [Preparation](#preparation)).
355	4. **Bump the version-of-record** to this commit's version
356	   (the suffix scheme is in
357	   [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)). The
358	   Preparation's own bump already covers a Preparation
359	   commit.
360	5. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step, skip-able
361	   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
362	   example the cargo cycle is:
363	   1. `cargo fmt`
364	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
365	   3. `cargo test`
366	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
367	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
368	6. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description,
369	   and tell the user "please review". The stop is its own
370	   message and carries no title or body, drafted or final: a
371	   description beside the work review collapses two stops
372	   into one, and describes work the review may still change.
373	   The user reviews the changes and we iterate until
374	   complete.
375	7. **Write the commit description**, only once the work
376	   review completes. See
377	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
378	8. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
379	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
380	9. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
381	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
382	   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
383	   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
384	   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate.
385	   Push approval is per-push, so step 8's
386	   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
387	   includes the push.
388	
389	**Two overrides apply:**
390	
391	- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
392	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
393	  surface it. Don't push through.
394	- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
395	  a review or question forward.
396	
397	## Commit description
398	
399	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
400	
401	```
402	<type>: <short description>
403	<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
404	```
405	
406	**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The
407	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
408	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you
409	are running the version you are testing. It is not an
410	identifier, and a commit already records it in the manifest.
411	Writing it into the description copies it into text that
412	cannot be edited: a version is only stable once it lands on
413	the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
414	renumber it, at which point every description naming it is
415	wrong forever. See
416	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
417	
418	### Title
419	
420	- Length per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths).
421	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
422	  `docs`, `chore`. Optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
423	  the type, per the spec.
424	- Favor terse phrasings.
425	- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
426	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
427	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
428	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them. The
429	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
430	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
431	- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the
432	  only identifier a record has, so it must be distinct
433	  within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header
434	  is also an anchor). It may repeat across the repo's
435	  history. See
436	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
437	
438	### Body
439	
440	A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
441	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped
442	per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths).
443	The problem statement says what was wrong and defines
444	any word the title assumes. The solution statement says what
445	was done about it. Content rules, including why the body
446	carries no file list, are in
447	[prose.md](prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.
448	
449	Two repo-specific points:
450	
451	- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the
452	  records' problem.
453	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe
454	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
455	
456	### Trailer
457	
458	`ochid:` as the last line of the body. See
459	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
460	in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.
461	
462	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
463	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
464	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows. The
465	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
466	
467	## Reviewing changes
468	
469	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
470	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
471	editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:
472	
473	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
474	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
475	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
476	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
477	
478	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
479	it mutable and shifts `@`. Use `jj diff -r @-` or
480	`jj show -r @-`.
481	
482	No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
483	wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
484	that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
485	runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.
486	
487	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
488	close-out squash recipe and recovery. Revset primitives
489	are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).
490	
491	## Pushing
492	
493	### Policy
494	
495	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
496	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
497	the cycle's result must be published.
498	
499	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
500	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
501	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
502	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
503	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
504	the push itself. Stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
505	
506	**Default is interactive; an explicit scoped delegation waives
507	the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
508	commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
509	the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
510	default*.
511	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
512	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
513	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
514	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
515	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
516	
517	- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
518	  well-scoped. The user's words must authorize unattended
519	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
520	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
521	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
522	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
523	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
524	  unattended") waives them.
525	- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only. It does not
526	  carry to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
527	- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
528	  ordinary commits and pushes. It does *not* pre-authorize a
529	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
530	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
531	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
532	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
533	  reaches this.
534	- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
535	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
536	- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
537	  per-push approval.
538	
539	**Delegation waives stops, never flow.** The stops (work review, description review, per-push
540	approval, the hard stop after the final push) are the synchronous half of review. The flow
541	(the records, the validation, the bookmark discipline) is what deferred review reads, so no
542	delegation waives it: a delegated cycle writes every record and validates every commit exactly
543	as an interactive one, and the user reviews after the fact what they would otherwise have
544	reviewed in real time. The tiers:
545	
546	- **Interactive** (the default): every stop, as above.
547	- **Delegated cycle**: rungs push to the topic bookmark without per-push asks; `main` is
548	  untouched by construction, so review happens at landing: read the line, then land it.
549	- **Delegated project**: landing is delegated too; review happens after, and corrections
550	  become new cycles.
551	
552	Destructive ops pause in every tier, and landing is its own tier, delegated separately.
553	
554	### Shape at close-out push
555	
556	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done; its *published
557	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
558	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
559	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
560	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
561	
562	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
563	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
564	  focused on one or two files.
565	- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
566	  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
567	  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
568	  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
569	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
570	  every rung stays reachable. See
571	  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
572	  for the full sequence.
573	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
574	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
575	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
576	  ladder refs, no consolidation churn.
577	
578	A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`; a trapezoid
579	is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
580	other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
581	
582	### Trapezoid close-out recipe
583	
584	A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
585	published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
586	two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
587	bookmark at the reshaped commit.
588	
589	```
590	  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
591	                      \                    /
592	  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
593	```
594	
595	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
596	  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
597	  first parent.
598	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
599	  second parent.
600	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
601	
602	The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`; the rest is jj,
603	because after step 1 the commits already exist and all that
604	remains is reshaping and publishing them:
605	
606	1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
607	   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
608	   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
609	2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
610	   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
611	   argument order.
612	3. `jj new <closeout>`
613	   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
614	4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
615	   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
616	   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
617	   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
618	   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
619	
620	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out
621	that tried it. Push runs its whole pipeline or
622	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
623	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
624	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
625	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
626	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
627	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
628	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
629	the latter is push's job.
630	
631	#### Details
632	
633	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
634	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
635	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
636	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive
637	  close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
638	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
639	  once published.
640	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
641	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
642	  and must stay there. Take the parent of the ladder's first
643	  rung, not the last close-out.
644	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
645	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
646	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
647	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
648	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
649	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
650	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
651	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
652	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
653	  publish; it leaves you working from the wrong parent.
654	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
655	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
656	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
657	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
658	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
659	  becomes unreachable, and anyone who fetched between the two
660	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
661	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
662	  SHA from that window. Wait until step 4 lands.
663	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
664	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
665	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
666	  push force-updates the target.
667	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
668	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
669	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
670	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
671	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
672	
673	#### Recovery
674	
675	- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
676	  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
677	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
678	  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
679	  Do not push a shape you did not intend. After step 4 the
680	  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
681	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
682	  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
683	  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
684	  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
685	  rebase onto the merge.
686	- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
687	  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
688	  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
689	  sideways move, not a rewrite.
690	
691	### vc-x1 push wrapper
692	
693	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
694	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
695	work-repo bookmark only. The bot repo is always pinned to
696	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
697	
698	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
699	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape. Other
700	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
701	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`.
702	This protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
703	
704	### .claude cadence
705	
706	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
707	with every work-repo commit in that push.
708	
709	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
710	across the cycle. Its change ID stays stable across
711	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
712	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
713	
714	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
715	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
716	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
717	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
718	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
719	
720	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
721	session information created, which we don't worry about.
722	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
723	remain empty.
724	
725	### Bot communication at the reviews
726	
727	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
728	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
729	
730	- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
731	  "Work complete. Please review." No title or body in this
732	  message: the description is not yet written, and belongs
733	  to the next review.
734	- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
735	  and `$BODY` explicitly, and ask permission to commit/push.
736	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
737	  --body ...` invocation by default.
738	- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
739	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target,
740	  then wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
741	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
742	
743	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
744	
745	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
746	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
747	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
748	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
749	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
750	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
751	
752	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
753	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
754	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
755	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
756	  turn's *final* push.
757	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
758	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
759	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
760	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
761	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
762	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
763	  user, after the turn, can capture it
764	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
765	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
766	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
767	  visible token after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare
768	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
769	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
770	  closing line after the push. That is a known slip.
771	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
772	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
773	  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
774	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
775	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
776	
777	### Recovery
778	
779	- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
780	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
781	  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:
782	
783	  ```
784	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
785	  ```
786	
787	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
788	  exit, with no log file to chase.
789	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
790	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
791	  agents).
792	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
793	    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
794	    closing response land after the squash.
795	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
796	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
797	    change. It is not under the user's control.)
798	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
799	    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
800	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
801	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
802	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
803	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
804	- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
805	  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
806	  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
807	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
808	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
809	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push. That is a
810	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
811	  push.
812	
813	## Iterative work
814	
815	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
816	from incremental review, loop:
817	
818	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
819	2. Make the next round of changes.
820	3. User reviews the round (see
821	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
822	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
823	   new empty `@`.
824	5. If not done, go to step 2.
825	
826	Same jj mechanics as a
827	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
828	single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.
829	
830	## Sub-cycle ladders
831	
832	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
833	[Step naming](#step-naming), and
834	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
835	manifest's suffix nests), its Work
836	commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
837	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
838	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
839	review and bisection only.
840	
841	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
842	
843	For each Work commit in the ladder:
844	
845	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
846	2. Do the commit's work.
847	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
848	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
849	   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
850	   full suite, raising bisection cost.
851	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
852	   only. The sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
853	   into one final commit.
854	
855	**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
856	[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
857	commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
858	once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
859	therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
860	rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
861	exception to
862	[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).
863	
864	### Navigating the ladder
865	
866	Common moves:
867	
868	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
869	  from its base.
870	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
871	  commit by chid prefix, useful for bisection.
872	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
873	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
874	  isolation.
875	
876	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place, and
877	descendants auto-rebase.
878	
879	### Close-out: squash the ladder
880	
881	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
882	
883	```
884	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
885	```
886	
887	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit, and `-u`
888	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
889	After squash, history is linear (`<base> -> @`), and
890	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
891	
892	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
893	the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
894	trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
895	of the
896	[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
897	never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
898	describing them freely is safe.
899	
900	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
901	when `@-` is `<base>`). Push the single commit directly.
902	
903	### Recovery
904	
905	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
906	prior commits:
907	
908	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
909	  drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
910	  parent.
911	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
912	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
913	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
914	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
915	  the op history, and `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
916	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
917	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
918	
919	# References
920	
921	- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
922	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
923	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
924	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
925	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
926	  bisection cost.
927
