2	
3	Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
4	wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).
5	
6	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
7	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
8	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Line width
11	
12	Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
13	prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
14	The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
15	comment text it doesn't reflow.
16	
17	## Doc comments on every file, function, and method
18	
19	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
20	a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
21	is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
22	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
23	
24	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
25	inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
26	explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
27	non-obvious WHY.
28	
29	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
30	by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
31	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
32	help.
33	
34	## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
35	
36	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
37	`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
38	patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
39	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
40	in scope:
41	
42	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
43	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
44	  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.
45	
46	When one is used, three obligations attach:
47	
48	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
49	  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
50	    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
51	  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
52	    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
53	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
54	    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
55	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
56	  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
57	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
58	  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:
59	
60	  ```toml
61	  [lints.clippy]
62	  unwrap_used = "warn"
63	  expect_used = "warn"
64	  ```
65	
66	  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
67	  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
68	  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
69	  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)
70	
71	```rust
72	let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
73	let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious
74	
75	match matches.len() {
76	    1 => {
77	        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
78	        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
79	        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
80	    }
81	    // ...
82	}
83	```
84	
85	Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
86	behavior.

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
comment text it doesn't reflow.

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional); a
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties, mandatory validation included. So a
19	single-step cycle is one commit, and a multi-step is minimum two (a Work commit plus the
20	close-out), typically three or more (the definition is
21	[AGENTS.md's Terminology](../AGENTS.md#terminology)). The
22	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
23	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
24	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
25	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
26	
27	## Cycles run on a bookmark
28	
29	A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work repo, created at the opening and named by the
30	cycle title's slug (the anchor algorithm in
31	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). `main` advances only when the
32	finished cycle lands on it; nothing pushes straight to `main`. The bot repo needs no bookmark:
33	its `main` rides the tip of its linear narrative.
34	
35	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
36	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
37	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
38	  that makes the cycle permanent.
39	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
40	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
41	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
42	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
43	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
44	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
45	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
46	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
47	
48	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
49	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
50	
51	## Opening checklist
52	
53	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
54	
55	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
56	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
57	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
58	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
59	   title, `####` items; under a program heading, each one deeper):
60	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
61	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
62	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
63	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
64	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
65	     `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`,
66	     unlinked until its gotchas subsection exists)
67	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
68	     deliberate)
69	   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, headed by the rung's
70	   exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs land; the
71	   closing rung's is created at close-out only if gotchas occurred (see the protocol's
72	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
73	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
74	   version-of-record.
75	
76	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
77	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
78	
79	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
80	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
81	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
82	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
83	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
84	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
85	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
86	
87	## Committing vs pushing
88	
89	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
90	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
91	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
92	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
93	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
94	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
95	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
96	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
97	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
98	
99	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
100	
101	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
102	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
103	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
104	
105	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
106	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
107	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
108	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
109	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
110	  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
111	  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
112	
113	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
114	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
115	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
116	
117	## Per-commit checklist
118	
119	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
120	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
121	
122	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
123	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
124	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
125	   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
126	   rung was laddered; the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
127	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
128	4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
129	   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
130	   commit.
131	5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
132	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
133	6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
134	   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
135	   review is likely complete.
136	7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a problem
137	   statement and a solution statement, both broad, sized per prose.md's
138	   [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
139	   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See
140	   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
141	8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
142	   explicitly includes it.
143	9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
144	   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
145	
146	## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist
147	
148	Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
149	[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):
150	
151	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
152	2. Do the commit's work.
153	3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
154	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
155	   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.
156	
157	Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
158	(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
159	publishes the single commit.
160	
161	## Before any push
162	
163	- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
164	  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
165	  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
166	  bounded task only. Delegation waives stops, never flow (records, validation, the bookmark
167	  discipline; see the protocol's [Policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy)), and destructive ops
168	  still pause.
169	- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
170	- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).
171	
172	## After the final push: hard stop
173	
174	Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
175	verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
176	words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
177	after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
178	or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
179	delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
180	push. See
181	[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).
182	
183	## Close-out checklist
184	
185	The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
186	[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):
187	
188	1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the

211	   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).

213	   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional); a
**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties, mandatory validation included. So a
single-step cycle is one commit, and a multi-step is minimum two (a Work commit plus the
close-out), typically three or more (the definition is
[AGENTS.md's Terminology](../AGENTS.md#terminology)). The
ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
work, and before any push, cycle or not.

## Cycles run on a bookmark

A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work repo, created at the opening and named by the
cycle title's slug (the anchor algorithm in
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). `main` advances only when the
finished cycle lands on it; nothing pushes straight to `main`. The bot repo needs no bookmark:
its `main` rides the tip of its linear narrative.

- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
  that makes the cycle permanent.
- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).

**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.

## Opening checklist

At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:

1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
   title, `####` items; under a program heading, each one deeper):
   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
   - **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
     `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`,
     unlinked until its gotchas subsection exists)
   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
     deliberate)
   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, headed by the rung's
   exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs land; the
   closing rung's is created at close-out only if gotchas occurred (see the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
   version-of-record.

Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
   rung was laddered; the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
   commit.
5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
   review is likely complete.
7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a problem
   statement and a solution statement, both broad, sized per prose.md's
   [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See
   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only. Delegation waives stops, never flow (records, validation, the bookmark
  discipline; see the protocol's [Policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy)), and destructive ops
  still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
   markers, add any design subsections, and write the closing rung's gotchas subsection
   (problem/solution form) if closing surfaced any.
3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.
   Four transforms, two of which fail silently: headings one level deeper, rung refs renumbered
   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes
   rewritten. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). Add the title-only
   `## Table of Contents` entry.
4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,
   detail as sub-bullets (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Replace the
   `## In Progress` block with `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
5. Full validation, mandatory.
6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
8. **Land the bookmark** on the user's go. Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent.
   Once `main` contains the bookmark, delete it, locally and remotely. See
   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
9. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for the
   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's
   share. Never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch. The backfill edits ride the next
   push (a commit cannot record its own SHA).

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports. Getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
4	suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
5	copied **verbatim**, with
6	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
7	conditional rather than per-project edits.
8	
9	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
10	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
11	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
12	
13	## Terms
14	
15	Three names, used as defined here across
16	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
17	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
18	
19	- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
20	  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
21	  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
22	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
23	  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
24	  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
25	- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
26	  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
27	  artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## A stamp, not a name
31	
32	The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
33	named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
34	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
35	suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
36	inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.
37	
38	## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides
39	
40	Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
41	touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**
42	
43	- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
44	  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
45	  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
46	  presentation, docs, notes.
47	- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
48	  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
49	- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
50	  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).
51	
52	**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
53	thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.
54	
55	## Grammar and storage
56	
57	One spelling everywhere the version is written:
58	
59	```
60	<public>[-<suffix>]
61	```
62	
63	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
64	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
65	  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
66	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
67	  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
68	  version storable in every medium below.
69	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
70	  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
71	  Cargo rejects one.)
72	
73	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
74	
75	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
76	  valid at any dot depth.
77	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
78	  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
79	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
80	  adds its case to
81	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
82	
83	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
84	
85	- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
86	  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
87	  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
88	  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
89	  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
90	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
91	  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
92	  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.
93	
94	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
95	multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
96	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
97	`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
98	silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
99	every medium accepts.
100	
101	## Recording the version-of-record
102	
103	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
104	the case that fits your medium:
105	
106	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
107	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
108	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
109	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
110	    ...). Add the case as needed
111	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
112	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
113	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
114	    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
115	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
116	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
117	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
118	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
119	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
120	  per-commit preference.
121	
122	## Dev artifact name
123	
124	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
125	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
126	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
127	
128	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
129	  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
130	  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
131	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
132	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
133	  install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
135	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
136	  flow's install.
137	
138	Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
139	its `custom.md` layer.
140	
141	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
142	
143	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
144	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
145	
146	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
147	  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
148	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
149	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
150	  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
151	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
152	
153	## Suffix scheme
154	
155	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
156	each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157	
158	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159	not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160	neither a number nor a version (see
161	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162	prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163	commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164	nothing dereferences one.
165	
166	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
168	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
conditional rather than per-project edits.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides

Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**

- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
  presentation, docs, notes.
- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).

**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
  version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
  Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
  valid at any dot depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
  adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

input.old_string:
#### Solution

Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
config surface from it:

- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
  reference url
- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
    code cannot disagree with the file
- each key's rendered block carries a `doc references:` list: the derived web url (a
  localfile entry joins at backlog #52, once init seeds the file it would point at)
- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
- retire the state-dir leftovers
- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
  active keys and `[repos]`
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
- repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`
  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record
input.new_string:
#### Solution

Adopt a markdown carrier for the config surface (wink, 2026-08-11), then rebuild the pipeline
on it. The format: a config file is a markdown document whose `toml` fences, concatenated in
document order, form the TOML the loader parses, so prose, per-key doc, and real reference
links live beside the keys they document. `test2-vc-config.md` is the model rendering
(compact: one fence per table, doc-link bullets above it).

- a md -> toml filter (non-fence lines blanked, so any diagnostics keep the source's line
  numbers) feeds the existing parser
  - the loader resolves `.vc-config.md`, still accepts `.vc-config.toml` for the family's
    migration window, and errors when a side has both
- the prototype `vc-config.toml` becomes `vc-config.md` in the same format: per-key `##`
  sections (the anchors the generated web urls land on) absorb `vc-config-design.md`, which
  retires, so the schema source and the browsable doc are one file
- the config surface adopts the agent vocabulary: `repos.agent`, `[agent-session]`, an
  `agent-session` subcommand and `--scope=agent`, old names accepted as aliases; the pinned
  prose sweep is a later convention cycle
- regenerate both sides' instance configs as `.vc-config.md`, retiring the fossil `[push]`
  comment blocks and the `.vc-x1` state-dir leftovers
- `config --refresh` regenerates the prose between fences while preserving fence interiors
  and `[repos]` byte-for-byte
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
- per-key worked examples in `vc-config.md`, so a reference link rewards the click
- repoint `repos.agent` at `.agent-session`
  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record

#### Acceptance check

1. build.rs generates the schema table and default constants from `vc-config.toml`
   (rerun-if-changed wired), the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP` constants are gone
   from `src/`, and generated configs carry each key's `doc references:` list (the derived web
   url per key).
2. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
3. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
4. `config --refresh --check` exits clean on both sides, proving the committed config files
   match what the prototype renders.
5. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
6. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
   dir under its new name.
7. `validate-anchors` runs clean over `TODO.md`, `notes/`, `README.md`, and `vc-config.md`
   (same-file heading anchors and `[N]` refs), and a test shows it catching a broken anchor.

791	/// Resolve a `Scope` to concrete repo paths.
792	///
793	/// - `Side::Work` -> `workspace_root` (or cwd's `.` when
794	///   `workspace_root` is None).
795	/// - `Side::Bot` -> the root config's `repos.bot`, resolved
796	///   file-relative against the root.
797	///
798	/// Errors when `Side::Bot` is requested but the workspace doesn't
799	/// define one (POR or single-repo workspace).
800	pub fn scope_to_repos(
801	    scope: &Scope,
802	    workspace_root: Option<&Path>,
803	) -> Result<Vec<PathBuf>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
804	    if let Some(root) = workspace_root {
805	        reject_legacy_config(root)?;
806	    }
807	    let mut repos = Vec::new();
808	    for side in &scope.0 {
809	        match side {
810	            Side::Work => repos.push(
811	                workspace_root
812	                    .map(Path::to_path_buf)
813	                    .unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from(".")),
814	            ),
815	            Side::Bot => {
816	                let root = workspace_root.ok_or(
817	                    "--scope=bot: not in a vc-x1 workspace (no .vc-config.toml with a \
818	                     [repos] registry), drop --scope or use --scope=work",
819	                )?;
820	                let cfg = toml_simple::toml_load(&root.join(VC_CONFIG_FILE))?;
821	                let bot = toml_simple::toml_get(&cfg, "repos.bot")
822	                    .filter(|v| !v.is_empty())
823	                    .ok_or(
824	                        "--scope=bot: no bot repo configured. Add `bot = \"...\"` to the \
825	                         [repos] registry to enable dual-repo operations",
826	                    )?;
827	                repos.push(resolve_repo_path(root, bot));
828	            }
829	        }
830	    }
831	    Ok(repos)
832	}
833	
834	/// Resolve the workspace's bot-repo path, or `None` when it has no
835	/// bot side.
836	///
837	/// The scope-aware prelude for commands that *optionally* work
838	/// against the bot repo (validate-desc / fix-desc): topology comes
839	/// from `default_scope` (the workspace config), not a flag:
840	/// `Ok(None)` means a POR / single-repo workspace, the caller's
841	/// no-op case, while a configured-but-broken bot side still errors
842	/// via `scope_to_repos`.
843	pub fn bot_repo_path(workspace_root: &Path) -> Result<Option<PathBuf>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
844	    match configured_bot_dir(workspace_root)? {
845	        Some(bot) => {
846	            verify_workspace_coherence(workspace_root, &bot)?;
847	            Ok(Some(bot))
848	        }
849	        None => Ok(None),
850	    }
851	}
852	
853	/// The bot dir the workspace config *declares*: a pure config
854	/// read, no on-disk verification.
855	///
856	/// The pre-coherence half of [`bot_repo_path`], for callers that
857	/// resolve the dir before it exists (clone names the local clone
858	/// destination from the just-cloned work repo's config). `Ok(None)`
859	/// when the workspace declares no bot side.
860	pub fn configured_bot_dir(
861	    workspace_root: &Path,
862	) -> Result<Option<PathBuf>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
863	    reject_legacy_config(workspace_root)?;
864	    if !default_scope(Some(workspace_root)).has_bot() {
865	        return Ok(None);
866	    }
867	    let repos = scope_to_repos(&Scope(vec![Side::Bot]), Some(workspace_root))?;
868	    match repos.as_slice() {
869	        [bot] => Ok(Some(bot.clone())),
870	        other => Err(format!(
871	            "configured_bot_dir: expected one repo from scope_to_repos, got {}",
872	            other.len()
873	        )
874	        .into()),
875	    }
876	}
877	
878	/// Resolve the bot repo of a workspace that *requires* one.
879	///
880	/// The dual-only sibling of [`bot_repo_path`] for operations that
881	/// make no sense without a bot side (push): `None` becomes a loud
882	/// error instead of a no-op signal.
883	pub fn require_bot_dir(workspace_root: &Path) -> Result<PathBuf, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
884	    bot_repo_path(workspace_root)?.ok_or_else(|| {
885	        format!(
886	            "{}/.vc-config.toml declares no bot repo (`repos.bot`): \
887	             this operation requires a dual workspace",
888	            workspace_root.display()
889	        )
890	        .into()
891	    })
892	}
893	
894	/// Dual-mode entry preflight: verify the two repos' recorded
895	/// topology agrees before any operation acts on it.
896	///
897	/// Checks, in order, erroring with everything known and changing
898	/// nothing (the dual-preflight principle, 2026-07-23):
899	///
900	/// - the bot dir exists (and is a directory);
901	/// - its `.vc-config.toml` loads;
902	/// - **resolved agreement**: each side's declared `[repos]` pair,
903	///   resolved file-relative and canonicalized, names the same two
904	///   directories (the file-relative schema makes the raw blocks
905	///   asymmetric by design, so agreement is checked on resolved
906	///   reality, not spelling);
907	/// - **self-identification**: each config's own directory sits at
908	///   its side's key (root's `work`, bot's `bot`): agreement
909	///   alone can't catch both sides naming the same wrong pair.
910	///
911	/// Mid-flight surprises stay per-operation concerns; this gates
912	/// *entry* at the one topology resolver.
913	fn verify_workspace_coherence(root: &Path, bot: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
914	    if !bot.is_dir() {
915	        return Err(format!(
916	            "workspace incoherent: {}/.vc-config.toml declares bot repo '{}', \
917	             but that directory does not exist, fix the `bot` value or \
918	             restore the directory; nothing was changed",
919	            root.display(),
920	            bot.display()
921	        )
922	        .into());
923	    }
924	    let root_cfg = toml_simple::toml_load(&root.join(VC_CONFIG_FILE))?;
925	    let bot_cfg = toml_simple::toml_load(&bot.join(VC_CONFIG_FILE)).map_err(|e| {
926	        format!(
927	            "workspace incoherent: bot repo '{}' has no readable {VC_CONFIG_FILE} \
928	             ({e}): both sides must carry a [repos] registry naming the same \
929	             directories; nothing was changed",
930	            bot.display()
931	        )
932	    })?;
933	    let (root_pair, bot_pair) = (
934	        resolved_repos_pair(root, &root_cfg)?,
935	        resolved_repos_pair(bot, &bot_cfg)?,
936	    );
937	    if root_pair != bot_pair {
938	        return Err(format!(
939	            "workspace incoherent: the two sides' [repos] registries resolve to \
940	             different directories: they must name the same work/bot pair; \
941	             nothing was changed\n\
942	             {}/{VC_CONFIG_FILE}: work={}, bot={}\n\
943	             {}/{VC_CONFIG_FILE}: work={}, bot={}",
944	            root.display(),
945	            root_pair.0.display(),
946	            root_pair.1.display(),
947	            bot.display(),
948	            bot_pair.0.display(),
949	            bot_pair.1.display()
950	        )
951	        .into());
952	    }
953	    // Self-identification: agreement alone can't catch both sides
954	    // naming the same *wrong* pair: each config's own directory
955	    // must sit at its side's key.
956	    let canon_root = root.canonicalize()?;
957	    if root_pair.0 != canon_root {
958	        return Err(format!(
959	            "workspace incoherent: {}/{VC_CONFIG_FILE}'s `repos.work` resolves to \
960	             '{}', not to the workspace root itself: the work side's own entry \
961	             must name its own directory; nothing was changed",
962	            root.display(),
963	            root_pair.0.display()
964	        )
965	        .into());
966	    }
967	    let canon_bot = bot.canonicalize()?;
968	    if bot_pair.1 != canon_bot {
969	        return Err(format!(
970	            "workspace incoherent: {}/{VC_CONFIG_FILE}'s `repos.bot` resolves to \
971	             '{}', not to the bot repo itself: the bot side's own entry must \
972	             name its own directory; nothing was changed",
973	            bot.display(),
974	            bot_pair.1.display()
975	        )
976	        .into());
977	    }
978	    Ok(())
979	}

982	///
983	/// The per-side half of the resolved-agreement check: reads

1007	                    "workspace incoherent: {}/{VC_CONFIG_FILE}'s `{key}` (\"{value}\") does \

1009	                    cfg_dir.display()
1010	                )
1011	                .into()
1012	            })

a comment linkifies nowhere, so a config could not link a reader to
its own docs. The cycle adopted a markdown carrier for the config
surface, prose and reference links beside the keys with the TOML in
fenced code blocks, and nothing could parse that carrier.

it:

- md_to_toml keeps toml-fence interiors, blanks every other line (so
  diagnostics keep the source's line numbers), errors on an unclosed
  fence, and ignores non-toml fences as illustration

  the family's migration window, and errors when a side holds both
- workspace detection, the resolvers, config --validate, and the
  schema hints all go through the one resolver, so a broken config
  surfaces loudly instead of degrading the workspace to a plain repo
- the schema drift test anchors into notes/vc-config-design.md until
  the absorb rung merges the doc into vc-config.md
```

content.text:
Honest answer: after this rung, the user-visible surface is real but narrow — the binary can now *read* the markdown form, and nothing yet *writes* it.

Supported today, from the user's chair:

1. **You can hand-convert an instance config to markdown.** Delete `.vc-config.toml`, write `.vc-config.md` in the model shape (`vc-config-test.md`), and every command works against it: workspace detection, `--scope` resolution, push's dual-repo topology, coherence checks, `config --validate`. The end-to-end test does exactly this on both sides.
2. **`config --validate <path>`** accepts a markdown config file as a path target, same unknown-key checking as toml.
3. **The both-carriers guard**: a side holding both files gets a loud, specific error instead of undefined behavior (it caught your draft within minutes of existing).
4. **Better failure behavior**: a broken config (bad fence, both carriers) errors at the resolvers instead of silently degrading the workspace to a plain repo.

Not yet supported — the rest of the ladder:

- Nothing *generates* a `.vc-config.md`: init still writes toml, `config` still prints the toml comment-block schema, and there's no refresh. The regenerate rung flips the workspaces; until then md is opt-in by hand.
- The prose and doc links inside a hand-written md config are entirely yours to author; the generated per-key doc with reference links arrives with the absorb + regenerate rungs.

```
The instance config is edited by the user, who needs to thoroughly
understand every aspect of it, and a toml file is limited in its
expressivity: documentation lives in # comment blocks, where typical
toml renderers do not allow linking to local documentation. The
cycle adopted a markdown carrier instead, prose and reference links
beside the keys with the tables and key/value pairs in fenced toml
code blocks, and nothing could parse that carrier.

  schema hints all go through the one resolver, so a broken config

content.text:
Both done in the records; here's each.

**The vc-x1-dev consequence.** The TODO section already carries it (the "consequence:" sub-bullet under the switch note). I've added it to the commit body's switch bullet:

**Body (the changed bullet only):**
```
- both sides of this workspace switch to hand-written .vc-config.md
  carriers here, dogfooding the handler for the rest of the cycle;
  the stable vc-x1 cannot resolve the workspace until a md-capable
  build promotes, so cycle operations run as vc-x1-dev meanwhile
```

The rest of the body stands as last shown.

**Priority when both are present — thoughts only:** I'd keep it exactly as built: a hard error, no priority, and I'd resist adding one later.

The argument: a precedence rule's failure mode is the worst one config systems have. Whoever edits the losing file gets silence — their change simply doesn't take effect, no error, no hint, and they burn an afternoon discovering the *other* file exists. That's the canonical "I changed the config and nothing happened" bug, and every tool with a config-form precedence ladder (ESLint is the famous offender) is notorious for it. An error, by contrast, is self-teaching: it fires at the first command, names both files, and says which one to keep.

The migration story doesn't need precedence either. A switch is write-`.md`, delete-`.toml`, one commit — and the error is precisely what catches a half-done switch, which it proved within minutes of existing by catching your morning draft sitting beside the live toml. With precedence, that draft would have silently *become* the workspace's config — a draft with no `[repos]` — and the failure would have surfaced somewhere far away as an unresolvable workspace.

There's also an asymmetry that favors the strict choice: adding precedence later, if a real need appears, is a small compatible change; removing precedence later, after people rely on it, is a breaking behavior change. Starting strict keeps both doors open.

The plain version: if both files exist we stop and tell you, rather than quietly picking one, because quietly picking one means someone someday edits the ignored file and nothing happens. Yes to saying the dev-binary fact in both places — the TODO had it, and the commit body now does too.

content.text:
Mystery solved, and your guess is exactly right — it's an echo the tool itself emits. `common::prompt` (src/common.rs:178) does this:

1. `eprint!("{msg}")` — prints the prompt to stderr, no newline; your typed `y` and Enter complete that line on screen. That's the first line.
2. After reading your answer: `info!("{msg}{trimmed}")` — re-prints the whole prompt *with your answer appended* through the logger. That's the second line.

The intent was presumably to get the prompt-and-answer pair into the logged record, since the raw `eprint!` bypasses the logger. But the logger also writes to stderr, so interactively both land in the same terminal and the replay is pure duplication — the live line already shows your keystroke via terminal echo.

So: not new, not this rung's doing, and harmless — but it is noise on every interactive push. The clean fix would be dropping the `info!` replay, or emitting it only when the answer needs to reach a non-terminal capture. I'd file it as a small bugs.md entry rather than touch it mid-rung; it's push-surface code and this commit is config-surface.

content.text:
Checked. The doubling lives in exactly one place — `common::prompt` — and all four interactive prompts in the tool flow through it: the two push-review stops (push.rs:314, :395), symlink's replace confirmation (symlink.rs:347), and sync's prompt (sync.rs:592). One fix covers everything. The other direct stderr prints are all deliberate and single-purpose (the logger's own warn/error routing, the version banner at main.rs:454, and test-only "preserving tempdir" notices), so nothing else has this pattern.

The logger explains why the replay exists and what the fix must preserve: `info!` goes to **stdout plus the optional log file**, while the live prompt goes to **stderr**. In a terminal, stdout and stderr are the same screen, so you see the line twice. But when stdout is captured — which is exactly how a bot session runs `vc-x1-dev push` — the `info!` replay is the *only* place the prompt-and-answer pair lands in the captured output, and the log file wants it too. So dropping the replay outright would blind the transcript case that this project itself depends on.

The fix that keeps both: route by whether stdout is a terminal (`std::io::IsTerminal`, stable std):

- stdout **is** a tty: replay at `debug!` — the log file still captures it (the file gets all levels), the console stays clean, and `-v` can still surface it deliberately.
- stdout is **not** a tty (piped, captured): replay at `info!` exactly as today, so transcripts keep recording the answer.

On sequencing, since it's push-surface code and the pending commit is the config handler: I'd make it its own small commit right after this one — `fix: prompt double echo in terminals` as an inserted rung — rather than burying it in the handler's diff. The implementation is a five-line change to one function; it can be written, validated, and pushed minutes after the handler lands.

So my proposal: approve the handler push now (`vc-x1-dev push docs-freshen-vc-config-and-config-subcmd`, description as last shown), and I'll do the prompt fix as the immediate next commit. Or if you'd rather it ride this commit despite the title mismatch, say so and I'll fold it in.

vc-x1-dev 0.78.8-5

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main`: one command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates.

Stages, in order:
  - review           approve the diff (first gate)
  - message          $EDITOR, or --title/--body; approve
                     the text (second gate). Skipped when
                     neither repo has pending changes
  - commit-work      commit the work repo. Skipped when
                     `@` is empty
  - commit-bot       commit `.claude`. Skipped when it is
                     clean
  - bookmark-set     work repo -> <bookmark>, bot -> main
  - push-work        publish <bookmark> to origin
  - squash-push-bot  fold `.claude`'s trailing writes
                     into its commit and push main

Rerunning is always safe: each stage does nothing when its
work is already done, so a failed run is re-run rather than
resumed. There is no saved state: vc-x1 cannot know why a
run failed, so it stops and reports. Please fix and try
again.

Failures in commit-work / commit-bot / bookmark-set roll both
repos back via `jj op restore` to a snapshot taken moments
earlier. Once push-work succeeds the work is published: from
there a change is either a new commit appended on top by the
next push, or an amend of what was pushed: `vc-x1
squash-push` folds the working copy into the last commit and
force-updates the remote.

vc-x1 runs no build or test steps: run your project's checks
yourself before pushing.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip both gates.

Usage: vc-x1-dev push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
